title: Uddalaka's clay: Brahman is what the world is made of
hook: Shvetaketu comes home proud, and his father teaches him with one lump of clay: Brahman is the clay as well as the potter.
carry: brahman is the clay as well as the potter
tomorrow: a god goes back to school four times. does anything stay?

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana met a person the size of a thumb: the one in your heart is Brahman itself. Today, the last day in the sutras, and a lump of clay.
screen: `SPACE IN A REED IS STILL SPACE.`

segments.voice: Shvetaketu was twelve when he left home to study the Vedas, and twenty-four when he came back: proud, sure he knew it all. His father, Uddalaka, saw it, and asked one question. Did you ask your teachers for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known? Shvetaketu had never heard of such a thing. What is it, sir? Near the end of their first chapter, the Brahma Sutras lean on the father's answer to settle a big question. If Brahman is the source of everything, is Brahman the potter, or the clay?
screen: `HOME AT TWENTY-FOUR, PROUD.` → `THE UNKNOWN, KNOWN?` → `THE POTTER, OR THE CLAY?`

segments.voice: The sutra's answer: both. Brahman is the material too, not only the maker. And it gives its reason from Uddalaka's answer. By one lump of clay, everything made of clay is known. The pot, the bowl, the lamp are names and shapes; the clay is what's real in them. Shankara presses the point. That promise, know one thing and know everything, only works if the one thing is what everything is made of. If Brahman were only the potter, knowing the potter wouldn't tell you the pots. The next sutra adds a clue. The texts say the source wished: may I be many. Nothing outside it is mentioned to become the many, so it becomes many from itself. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings. God isn't only a maker standing outside the world. In Shankara's reading, Brahman is what the world is made of. It's the root of a familiar Hindu instinct: to honor the sacred in a river, a guest, every living being. Jnana, here, isn't learning a long list of things. It's knowing the one clay, so the pots stop being strangers to each other. Ramanuja and Madhva read these same sutras differently, and their followers still do.
screen: `BOTH THE MAKER AND THE MATERIAL.` · `ONE LUMP OF CLAY, ALL CLAY KNOWN.` · `MAY I BE MANY.` · `BRAHMAN IS WHAT THE WORLD IS MADE OF.` · then, large: `THE POTS STOP BEING STRANGERS.`

segments.voice: Hold or look at one cup, bowl or mug near you. Take in its shape first, the rim, the handle, the chip if it has one. Then let the shape soften in your attention, and notice what it's made of, the same stuff as the other cups in the cupboard, wearing a different name.
Jnana: knowledge that frees. For Shankara, knowing the one clay, so the many are known.
For the road: Brahman is the clay as well as the potter. The sutras, complete.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, the clay example of the Chandogya Upanishad is often used to teach that Brahman is both the maker and the material of the world; Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita teachers read the same sutras in their own ways.

fork.setup: Uddalaka promises his proud son a teaching by which the unknown becomes known. you're Shankara. why does that promise need Brahman to be the clay, not only the potter?
options: knowing the potter wouldn't tell you the pots; knowing the clay does.
because potters are less important than the things they make.
it doesn't; the promise works either way.
fork.reveal: Know one thing and know everything only works if the one thing is what everything is made of. So the sutra says Brahman is the material too.

original.note: Sanskrit mrittika, clay or earth; the Chandogya's example of the one stuff in every pot.

what a scholar hears: Brahma Sutra 1.4.23–24: Brahman as material as well as efficient cause, so as not to break the Chandogya's promise and example (6.1.4), and from the wish 'may I be many'.

chat.meaning: Uddalaka taught that by one lump of clay all clay things are known; the pots keep their names and shapes, and the clay is real in them. For Shankara, Brahman is that clay as well as the potter.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–6 (Uddalaka asks Shvetaketu about the teaching by which the unheard is heard; by one lump of clay all that is made of clay is known; the change is a name; the clay is real)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.2.3; Taittiriya Upanishad 2.6 (the source wished: may I be many)
